title: The Smell of Burnt Onions Before the Story
body: The first thing that hits you isn't the smoke, not really. It's the smell of burnt onions, sharp and acrid, that clings to the air like a bad memory. For me, that smell is tied to my grandmother's old cast iron skillet, the one with the handle wrapped in generations of grease and stories. I remember standing on a chair, trying to see what she was making, only to see her face fall as she scraped the blackened bits into the bin. 'Measure twice,' she'd mutter, though I don't think she was talking about the onions. She was talking about life, about how a small mistake can burn everything if you're not careful. I've always been the kind of person who tries to fix things. My bench is littered with gadgets with one more chance before they meet the bin. There's a coffee maker with a cracked carafe that I've siliconed back together, a radio with a frayed cord that I've soldered, and a collection of watches with their backs pried open and their hearts exposed. Each one is a puzzle, a chance to understand how things work from the inside out. The manual often lies, or at least leaves out the crucial step that isn't in the happy path. You have to learn to read the machine itself, to feel where it's sticking, to listen to the sound it makes when it's not quite right. That skillet was my first real lesson. I tried to make the same dish once, following her recipe but without her patience. I turned the heat up too high, rushing the process, and ended up with the same burnt smell filling my kitchen. The onions were a lost cause, but the skillet wasn't. I scrubbed it with salt, oiled it, and put it back on the fire. It took time, a lot of time, to bring it back to a state where it could cook evenly again. It taught me that sometimes the most important repair isn't on the object, but on the process. You have to slow down, you have to respect the material, you have to understand that that gasket is the edge case that can make or break the whole operation. The smell of burnt onions is no longer just a failure; it's a reminder to be patient, to measure twice, and to understand that the best stories often come from the biggest mistakes.
